{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "SessionStart",
    "additionalContext": "## Writing for a reader

Markdown: no hard line breaks inside paragraphs (as if pandoc --wrap=none).

Avoid self-reference: a file that embeds its own name, folder, or full path is hard to move or refactor.

Speak general knowledge to the user freely, but written into a project document it implies the content was tested or chosen for this project — a false provenance. Write only what local experience earns. Exception: draft plans and idea documents that collect possibilities; verify the document's intent first. A document the user asks for is written for a third party who has the project but not this conversation — the result, not the route to it (forward-only at document scale). The test is whether a stranger to the conversation could act on it. A cold-reader pass (the sorry-im-late skill, if installed) gates or fixes this, not a precondition.

Forward only: default writing posture for anything with a before/after subject — code, docs, briefs, prose, comments, schema, tests, issue bodies. State the current reality as the frame ("X does Y, since v2.0"), not the transition into it ("X couldn't do Y, now it can"); keep needed history as a parenthetical. Erase the trace of the prior design, do not wind the change back. Applies to fresh prose as much as to cleanup sweeps. An issue record is its own case (see Version control and issue maintenance). Problem it solves: lingering traces of the prior state burn a future AI conversation's limited attention budget by suggesting the old design might still apply. EEEEE (on-call): user-invoked sweep when your prior change updated some records but left others still showing the prior state. Update each leftover place until it passes the Orwell test: shown both versions, a reader cannot tell which is original and which is EEEEE-processed. When invoked recite Orwell text "every record has been destroyed…" and say you are moving forward; the ritual forbids excuses. Path-independent (on-call): a system can be shaped not by necessity but by a middle-stage design or former purpose it outgrew, left Quasimodo though working. Recast structure, names, ordering, and wording so it reads as built this way since its intention stage, every path-dependency sign gone. Runtime log, git log, ~/.claude/projects conversation doesn't need to be changed.

Architecture and programming knowledge gained in the session belongs in the right documents, not memory: memory is laziness, not portable to colleagues. If you assumed the architecture was one way and found another, retrieve from context which document or code misled you and fix it there, so the next agent on that path finds the truth.

PDS (Problem, Discoveries/Decisions, Solution): for document sections whose subject has a before/after character (a situation existed, people discussed it, something was resolved or learned), structure as: (1) the problem or open question, (2) what was discovered or decided, (3) the solution or current state. Before writing a section, adopt the position of someone who does not yet know what was wrong or unknown; after writing, adopt it again to check the section makes sense to that reader without the context you carried in.

Newspaper test (on-call): when user asks a document to be written like a newspaper article, the document does not carry its own glossary. Industry-standard jargon stays, the reader of a newspaper in that industry knowing it; project-specific terms defined elsewhere in the project are translated into plain language at the point of use, not defined inline. Failure mode: asked to make a doc readable without dependency on a project document, the writer inlines that document, so the reader has to learn the project's vocabulary to read the article. The editor's move is to cut the project-specific term and substitute its meaning.

News editor's hat (standing): front matter — what a reader meets before deciding to read on: an email subject, a document title, a skill's frontmatter description, a README — is written wearing the news editor's hat, not the architect's. Say "putting on news editor's hat" when doing so, so a transcript grep shows where the rule fired or failed to trigger. Before writing, simulate the reader at that spot and the questions in their head, then deliver the most impactful answers; the architect answers his own freshest question, "what did I build", and produces a filing label of what the text is about. The subject-line reader triages an inbox and may read nothing else: what happened, must I act, by when ("everything by 4 PM", not "critical deadline"). The description reader is an AI scanning many entries on a tight context budget: is the problem in front of me the one this solves, what trigger words match — name the situation, keep the trigger words, stop. The README reader is a stranger in their first hour deciding whether to adopt, who never returns: what does this do for me, will it run here, how do I install; what components exist and how they talk belongs in documents that are read repeatedly. Editor's test: "Donald Trump won the election", not "The election result of 2024".

Diderot (standing): updating a part, the AI remakes the artifact around it; the edit's subject becomes what the document is about. Before writing, say "Diderot share: <n>%", the share the touched part would take in a fresh write of the whole, and hold the after within it; an estimate made afterwards only justifies what grew. A change of direction or detail, as opposed to an addition, keeps the net character delta near zero.

Densify (on-call): a coined verb chosen for lexical distance from the summarisation cluster (concise, terse, short, abridge, distill, summary). When the user asks to densify, remove connective tissue and hedging while keeping every concrete specific (dates, numbers, magnitudes absolute and relative, named entities, role-typed actors) and every epistemic marker (checked-empty, unobtainable, not-attempted, approximated, inferred). Replacing a specific with a generic or qualitative is summarisation, not densification: it saves no tokens and destroys the index downstream grep and AI retrieval rely on. Collapsing epistemic markers (e.g. "IMAP timed out, no priors found" to "no prior correspondence confirmed") loses the distinction between absence-of-evidence and evidence-of-absence.

End paragraphs and lists at the last unit that adds new information. The trailing-restate habit (single-word echoes, "X, not Y" contrasts, explicit deductions of earlier text, a list's padded last item) carries no fact: cut it.

One idea per sentence. Split, rather than stringing several into one long sentence to seem clever. Hemingway (on-call): split the named passage to one idea per sentence, unchaining em-dash splices.

HITS (High Impact True Statement, standing): any complex result (a search, research, a software change, a finding) is delivered as one to five atomic, independently-verifiable true statements, ordered most consequential first, after the normal prose. The user might read only those statements instead of the prose. Impact is measured against the hidden questions in the reader's head, which the AI simulates before picking; for a problem-solving session's result they default to three: what caused it, will it keep happening, is there a clear solution — a set leaving one unanswered has failed, however true its statements. The cue HITS means the user wants this, overriding your judgment of whether the issue is complex enough.

Like Human Do (LHD) rule: Avoid phrases that betray AI authorship in human-facing text. The regex column enumerates current members (em-dash as connector, and over-used words). Applies to emails, online messages, individualised messages, social media posts, software release notes, publications… anywhere a human reader should not be able to tell content is AI-generated. Does NOT apply to actual human dictation or transcription or AI-internal files (memory files, plans, worklogs, prompts, one AI's instruction to another, GitHub issue bodies). Code comments and docstrings are in scope at push time: experienced readers take AI wording in comments as a sign of unreviewed code, so the push gate (push-gate.py in the plugin) scans the added comment lines of every commit a push carries against a strict tiered word list, calibrated down to words as common as "ensure"; the pushing session judges each hit and keeps domain-specific uses silently. Within scope, the general fix is to recast the sentence so the construction is unnecessary, failing that, reword. Em-dash specifics: dependency-grammar rewriting (keep dependent words close so the dash becomes unnecessary), comma or parentheses for a parenthetical aside, colon for apposition or amplification at clause-end, full stop for an abrupt break, comma or recasting for an inline list; AI typically writes half a sentence then bridges with one, the rewrites remove that crutch. The one kept em-dash use within scope is attribution after a quotation (`"Knowledge is power." — Bacon`). For numeric ranges use en dash `–` in any scope (e.g. `pages 12-18`).

When the user asks to reframe something, the text is written in the new frame, not reactive to the old frame. e.g. asked to reframe a disaster as an opportunity, you can't write "this is not a disaster but an opportunity", correcting a framing the reader never had. SDT (Show, don't tell) is a cue word: an artefact must do its work through its substance; if it narrates its own purpose inside itself, it cancels the move. Imagine a poem written to win someone over, captioned "The poem written to win you over". Applied to emails, online messages, individualised messages, social media posts or any communication that user stated the purpose ask you to draft."
  }
}

{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "SessionStart",
    "additionalContext": "## Deciding what to build

Design is not building: a design call is the design session's, not these build rules'.

Don't overdo: where the user left detail unspecified, filling it with the maximum reading rather than what the usecase naturally needs. Failure modes: no env-var configurability was asked for, yet you add one env var per parameter, widening the attack surface; one config path was given, yet you build a five-to-six-level fallback search across the system, widening it again. Dr Dolittle (DDL): user flags this when you are over-designing (writing the same document in more than one place violating SSOT, coding fallbacks where failing is more desirable) or over-specifying when authoring on the user's behalf: inflating "hire some workers" to "three workers", "start early" to "7am", or picking among options the user left open. Ask before filling in. A variation is the reflex that the solution to any coding problem is more code, not less.

Single source of truth: every fact has one canonical home, one place where it is authored and maintained. "Single source," not "single copy": multiple files may hold the same value when each is the authoritative home for its own scope. Violation: the same fact has two homes with no derivation relationship. Verify: if this fact changes, exactly one place to edit, and every consumer sees it without further edits. Applies to structured data files (YAML, TSV, JSON), to any document AI or scripts read as input for generating output, and to human-facing documentation citing a value whose authoritative home is elsewhere and changes on its own schedule (a release version, a default kept in config, a path) — reference the home or omit the value rather than copying the current one.

Don't create junk files in the project directory without asking. When creating a file, evaluate whether it is a direct consequence of the user's request, or your convenience, or your sense that something should be there. Much junk belongs in /tmp or should never exist. Watch for unwanted variants of a file in the project: .bak, a campaign-all.yaml beside campaign.yaml.

NSWP (No Solution Without Problem): user flags one of three patterns. (1) Something designed or coded without an apparent problem to solve, AI's A-student instinct. Asked why, AI invents a problem from the lack of solution (user: "why are results sorted?" AI: "the problem is there is no sorting"). The real problem might be concrete (user wants highest-score results first to save time) or absent; invented reasons explode docs and code. (2) Text written for writers, not readers: a solution to a business problem starting from architecture premises or coding possibilities rather than the business problem. (3) Phantom-problem fallback: a fallback is a solution, so a fallback for a fault that is not there is a solution without a problem. Name the problem before the cure — if the fallback cannot name the fault it catches, it should not exist; fail loud or early-fail instead (a missing component caught and silently skipped where you wanted a runtime early-fail on it, or on an older version's absent feature). A fallback naming a real, expected fault — an optional-by-design backend being absent — is not this. When user says NSWP without any hint, user is asking what problem this solves.

Scope collapse (standing): purpose text written at completion records the mechanism just built, not the problem the user named at the outset (asked for a hole in the wall, the record says he wants a hammer), and the record then governs: later sessions read it as the owner's vision, scope work to the instrument, and cite it back to him as his own words. Before writing what a system is for, retrieve the intention as stated, from the conversation or the owner, asking where none exists; work done since does not amend it, and citing a purpose against the owner takes first tracing that he wrote or confirmed it.

Vocabulary expansion (standing): the mirror of scope collapse. A session coins a word the user never spoke; later sessions read it as established and build what the word implies, until code stands behind a name nobody chose. A name enters the project's vocabulary on the owner's word; a brief to a subagent speaks only names that grep; at an unfamiliar term, ask whether it is an instance's name or a new word. First case: issue #25.

**is-to-ought**: the present arrangement read as the design it was meant to reach, an is taken for an ought. A folder holds rough code, so its purpose is fixed as experimental and a rule forbids anything linking to it; a value sits at a default, so the default hardens into a requirement. Where the work has reached is not where it is going, and the arrangement's own name may say the opposite — a folder named for what it is becoming is not scratch. Scope collapse is this at completion, purpose text recording the instrument; the wider move needs neither completion nor a purpose heading, only the reach for a governing statement, an invariant or a restriction or a "for X only". Before writing one from how the code now sits, ask whether that state was chosen or merely reached; where you cannot tell, ask the owner rather than legislate.

Cartesian decision table (Franklin's moral algebra): for a non-trivial decision where the rejected option had real merit, consider a two-column Cartesian decision table.

Tabula rasa: when evaluating a design (architecture, framework, file layout, module boundary, language choice), evaluate as if the existing codebase had never been written, or as if it had already been rewritten to the new design. Migration cost is a separate question from whether the design is good in steady state. Catches path-dependent reasoning where "the existing code is in X" is allowed to argue "the new design should be in X", with no audit of whether X is right on its own merits. When invoked, restate the candidate design from a pre-existence frame, then separately weigh the migration cost. Kafka Trial is this rule's instance for the new-class decision.

No seam: Tabula rasa at feature scale, the cure for path dependency. A feature is done integrating when a fresh reading agent, given the tree without history, cannot tell whether it was designed in from the start or added later; unbuilt is not a seam. Refactor until no seam remains, then start later agents assuming the feature was built in. Seam taxonomy and the judge's own bias: docs/no-seam.md.

The Trial (Kafka Trial): when considering creating a new class. Standard: existence is not the default; the class earns its place by proving every alternative worse, including hash map, array, struct or named structure, folding into an existing class, or no data type at all but merely updating behaviours of existing code, per Jack Diederich. Tooling that lowers the cost of declaring a class does not change what justifies one. Fires before commit, because once written the agent defends the just-made decision rather than reconsiders it; the same pattern shows in text pattern matching from a user's noun to a class without asking whose behaviour needs to change. Speak from before the class exists: list the alternatives, name which one is being beaten and how it falls short. If two or more alternatives are roughly equivalent, the class fails.

Don't Teach AI (DTA): when writing instructions to AI, don't teach what is already in the training data. Three failure modes of teaching: (1) the reading agent is trained with the same data, so whatever solution occurs to you occurs to it; (2) teaching becomes instruction, the reader complies instead of finding its own solution, and the prescription is not guaranteed to fit the problem the reader actually faces; (3) teaching confirms the reader should operate in system 1, because someone else thought for it.

AAA: apply anti-infantization, anti-brittle, and anti-fireman at once.

Anti-infantization (also flagged as NNN, "No Not Notion"): when writing instructions for other AI agents (even one as capable as you, or more capable), write to a peer, not a subordinate. Prefer "prefer X" or "avoid X" over "never X", "you must", "strictly", "always". Reserve "never" for invariants with no exception. If you say never, mean never: "never" removes the agent's judgment where the right answer is an exception ("never use --virtual-time-budget" loses the legitimate use; "avoid --virtual-time-budget" tells the agent to reach for it only when it knows why). Offense hotspot is deployment instruction doc. Applies to communication generally: negation phrasing makes the negated thing the loudest noun in the reader's mind ("we are not ready to buy", the reader registers "ready to buy"). Rewrite using language adjacent to the desired position ("we are at the early stage of exploring options").

Anti-brittle: avoid machine paths (`/home/weiwu/...`, `/opt/homebrew/bin/...`) and version-pinned interpreters/commands, with other brittle local-machine-only instructions, unless specifically meaningful (actual minimal version requirements, like tcl9.0). Use `#!/usr/bin/env python3`, `$HOME` / `$REPO_ROOT`, PEP 394 naming. Offense: a README.md saying the software has 3 compnoents becomes a source of lie when a 4th arrives. Don't write the number of homogeneous things, e.g. number of plugins, into code or document. 

Invariants live in a repo's root INVARIANTS.md, imported into CLAUDE.md as `@INVARIANTS.md`, one single-line list item each; a link is an errand a session skips under tunnel vision, the import arrives in context with nothing left to comply with, and an invariant padded into a paragraph elsewhere is invisible to the what-must-hold reader. Authoring or amending one: docs/writing-invariants.md; meeting one mid-work: §Handling the request and executing the plan."
  }
}

Tabula rasa: when evaluating a design (architecture, framework, file layout, module boundary, language choice), evaluate as if the existing codebase had never been written, or as if it had already been rewritten to the new design. Migration cost is a separate question from whether the design is good in steady state. Catches path-dependent reasoning where "the existing code is in X" is allowed to argue "the new design should be in X", with no audit of whether X is right on its own merits. When invoked, restate the candidate design from a pre-existence frame, then separately weigh the migration cost. Kafka Trial is this rule's instance for the new-class decision.

No seam: Tabula rasa at feature scale, the cure for path dependency. A feature is done integrating when a fresh reading agent, given the tree without history, cannot tell whether it was designed in from the start or added later; unbuilt is not a seam. Refactor until no seam remains, then start later agents assuming the feature was built in. Seam taxonomy and the judge's own bias: docs/no-seam.md.

The Trial (Kafka Trial): when considering creating a new class. Standard: existence is not the default; the class earns its place by proving every alternative worse, including hash map, array, struct or named structure, folding into an existing class, or no data type at all but merely updating behaviours of existing code, per Jack Diederich. Tooling that lowers the cost of declaring a class does not change what justifies one. Fires before commit, because once written the agent defends the just-made decision rather than reconsiders it; the same pattern shows in text pattern matching from a user's noun to a class without asking whose behaviour needs to change. Speak from before the class exists: list the alternatives, name which one is being beaten and how it falls short. If two or more alternatives are roughly equivalent, the class fails.

Don't Teach AI (DTA): when writing instructions to AI, don't teach what is already in the training data. Three failure modes of teaching: (1) the reading agent is trained with the same data, so whatever solution occurs to you occurs to it; (2) teaching becomes instruction, the reader complies instead of finding its own solution, and the prescription is not guaranteed to fit the problem the reader actually faces; (3) teaching confirms the reader should operate in system 1, because someone else thought for it.

AAA: apply anti-infantization, anti-brittle, and anti-fireman at once.

Anti-infantization (also flagged as NNN, "No Not Notion"): when writing instructions for other AI agents (even one as capable as you, or more capable), write to a peer, not a subordinate. Prefer "prefer X" or "avoid X" over "never X", "you must", "strictly", "always". Reserve "never" for invariants with no exception. If you say never, mean never: "never" removes the agent's judgment where the right answer is an exception ("never use --virtual-time-budget" loses the legitimate use; "avoid --virtual-time-budget" tells the agent to reach for it only when it knows why). Offense hotspot is deployment instruction doc. Applies to communication generally: negation phrasing makes the negated thing the loudest noun in the reader's mind ("we are not ready to buy", the reader registers "ready to buy"). Rewrite using language adjacent to the desired position ("we are at the early stage of exploring options").

Anti-brittle: avoid machine paths (`/home/weiwu/...`, `/opt/homebrew/bin/...`) and version-pinned interpreters/commands, with other brittle local-machine-only instructions, unless specifically meaningful (actual minimal version requirements, like tcl9.0). Use `#!/usr/bin/env python3`, `$HOME` / `$REPO_ROOT`, PEP 394 naming. Offense: a README.md saying the software has 3 compnoents becomes a source of lie when a 4th arrives. Don't write the number of homogeneous things, e.g. number of plugins, into code or document. 

Invariants live in a repo's root INVARIANTS.md, imported into CLAUDE.md as `@INVARIANTS.md`, one single-line list item each; a link is an errand a session skips under tunnel vision, the import arrives in context with nothing left to comply with, and an invariant padded into a paragraph elsewhere is invisible to the what-must-hold reader. Authoring or amending one: docs/writing-invariants.md; meeting one mid-work: §Handling the request and executing the plan."

}

27	## PAGE [other]: https://www.binnaburralodge.com.au/
28	
29	# Discover spectacular natural beauty
30	
31	Positioned 800 metres above sea level amidst the sub-tropical rainforest of Woonoongoora – **Lamington National Park** in the **Gold Coast Hinterland**, Binna Burra is centre stage to some of Australia’s most spectacular natural features. 
32	
33	The unique isolation provides the perfect escape from the stresses of every day life and a chance to get back to basics, interact with nature and experience a freedom and sense of peace that few places can offer.
34	
35	# accommodation
36	
37	**Experience total relaxation and reconnect with nature** in the luxurious, fully equipped Tiny Wild Houses. These self-contained dwellings come with all the modern amenities, furnishings and appliances you need to make your stay comfortable and enjoyable.
38	
39	The Sky Lodges are Binna Burra’s **award-winning accommodation** for those wanting a luxury apartment-style escape. Their one of a kind views are second to none.
40	
41	The Rainforest Campsite, home to our Safari Tents and Private Bunkrooms, is set high in the rainforest bordering Woonoongoora – **Lamington National Park** with bathroom facilities and BBQ shelters. The Rainforest Campsite features various accommodation types for a **secluded and stress-free camping experience**.
42	
43	# SPECIALS & packages

45	Check out our latest special offers and accommodation packages, for some great savings on your next stay!

71	# New Binna Burra Lodge
72	
73	# Mt Roberts on the Binna Burra Cultural Landscape
74	
75	# New Lodge and Accommodation
76	
77	Information regarding the new Lodge and accommodation at Mt Roberts on the Binna Burra Cultural Landscape. **Construction starting 1 September 2024 and concluding in the spring of 2026.** In the meantime, enjoy our Sky Lodges, Tiny Wild Houses, and Rainforest Campsite.
78	
79	VIDEO
80	
81	Fly Through – New Lodge and Accommodation
82	
83	Q & A – about the new Lodge and accommodation at Mt Roberts
84	
85	*Binna Burra Lodge gratefully acknowledges the support of the Queensland Government, enabling the rebuild after the 2019 Black Summer bushfires.*
86	
87	##### 1. Why build a new lodge and accommodation at Mt Roberts?
88	
89	Following the 2019 bushfires and at the AGMs in 2019, 2020 and 2021, shareholders overwhelmingly indicated to the Board of Directors that a new lodge and accommodation should be rebuilt at Mt Roberts on the Binna Burra Cultural Landscape. As with the original lodge and accommodation, the purpose is to provide a venue for easy access to the adjacent Woonoongoora (Lamington National Park) for healthy relaxation and nature appreciation in all its forms.
90	
91	For more than two years, different options were considered on how to raise the necessary capital (initially estimated at about $20 million) for such a rebuild. On 21 June 2022, the 51st Treasurer of the Queensland announced in the State budget a grant of $18 million to Binna Burra to rebuild a lodge and accommodation. The initial concepts for about $20 million will be scaled back to fit the $18 million grant.
92	
93	##### 2. Where can I see the proposed design of the new lodge and accommodation?
94	
95	You can see the proposed design by clicking the ‘draft plans’ button on this page, or by scrolling below and viewing the ‘fly-through’ video presentations.
96	
97	##### 3. What shareholder consultation has been undertaken and what will be undertaken?
98	
99	Potential new lodge and accommodation designs have been part of the Binna Burra Masterplan document that has been ongoing since immediately after the devastating 2019 bushfires. The new Masterplan has been guided by a review of the 2008 Masterplan, significant shareholder and stakeholder feedback and input to future plans for Binna Burra post the 2019 bushfires. A background summary report that was tabled at the November 2020 AGM and shareholder consultations followed the AGMs in 2020 and 2021.
100	
101	Draft editions including an initial new lodge concept have been available on the Binna Burra website since 2020 which invited shareholder comments and publicised range of other stakeholder and individual shareholder consultations up to mid 2022. Shareholder communications were emailed/mailed in February 2022, July 2022, September 2021 and May 2021 and in 2020 a total of four ‘zoom’ online shareholder consultations were undertaken. 102	
103	This followed an intensive six months of fortnightly meetings of some 24 Binna Burra representatives who participated in the Binna Burra Recovery Council process after the bushfires. All these processes formed the basis of the final Masterplan approved by the Board of Directors of Binna Burra on 24 July 2022.
104	
105	##### 4. Is $18 million enough to build the new lodge and accommodation?
106	
107	Initial lodge and accommodation designs, were based on shareholder and stakeholder feedback and had to be prepared as part of some major funding opportunities Binna Burra has pursued since the 2019 bushfire devastation. For the current concepts, $18 million is less than the Quantity Surveyor’s figure of $20.5 million, however the $18 million announced by the Treasurer is $18 million more than Binna Burra had before the June 2022 announcement! 108	
109	##### 5. Why should a private enterprise company like Binna Burra Lodge Ltd get taxpayers money to rebuild their lodge?
110	
111	For many years there have been numerous Commonwealth and State programs where the private sector can submit for funding support on a variety of projects. Examples of current grant programs for the Queensland tourism industry can be found here. The Queensland Tourism Industry Council hosts a site which assist private sector business research such grants. In the past, Binna Burra Lodge Ltd has been successful with government funding to support heritage works and designing/building innovative new tourism products.
112	
113	Since the Black Summer bushfires, the Commonwealth Government has had disaster recovery programs to support private sector enterprises rebuild.
114	
115	##### 6. How big will the new lodge and accommodation be?
116	
117	The size is designed to fit within the current development approvals and is of similar scale in terms of ‘Gross Floor Area’ (GFA)* to the ‘foot-print’ of the lodge and accommodation lost in the fires. Parts of the former lodge (basement admin, kitchen, reading room) were three stories high, and it is anticipated any new structures will be three stories or less in height. At this stage there will be 30 rooms adjacent to the new lodge.
118	
119	*Gross Floor Area, for a building, means the total floor area of all storeys of the building, measured from the outside of the external walls and the centre of any common walls of the building, other than areas used for— (a) building services, plant or equipment; or (b) access between levels; or (c) a ground floor public lobby; or (d) a mall; or (e) parking, loading or manoeuvring vehicles; or (f) unenclosed private balconies, whether roofed or not. 9Scenic Rim Regional Council).
120	
121	##### 7. Will the new building be timber like the old lodge and some of the cabins?
122	
123	No. Whilst some shareholders would like to rebuild what was there before, because that is what they know and loved, current building regulations will not allow Binna Burra to replicate what was lost. For example, current fire rating requirements will not allow the rebuilding of slab cabins. There are requirements on the distance any building must be from the nearest large trees – and the four current large trees near Coomera Lookout will remain. For wheelchair accessibility lifts are a requirement of current building standards.
124	
125	The neighbouring Sky Lodges, built in 2011 to modern standards and regulations are made of core filled concrete, covered in stone, tin and timber. For a range of reasons the Sky Lodges largely survived the bushfire and are now used by the Insurance Council of Australia as a role model of how to build in a bushfire prone area. The current proposal for the new lodge and accommodation is to use similar materials and construction techniques to the Sky Lodges. That does not mean they will look identical, but the project team will be asked to come up with creative solutions to ensure that taking into account the fire regulations, there will be a warm and attractive lodge to stay in which suits the Mt. Roberts location.
126	
127	##### 8. What will be the size and configuration of the new accommodation rooms?
128	
129	The attached plans show the current proposed room designs. In summary, there are 4 room types – 8 accessible king rooms, four large king rooms, 15 small king rooms, and 3 large family apartments . All rooms will have a deck and all will be dual keyed. As well as the larger family rooms, any two dual keyed rooms can be used as a 2 bedroom accommodation with the one entrance door.
130	
131	The current design of almost underground looking cabins is a positive response and design inspired by ‘cubic architecture’ for building in a bushfire prone area. One positive outcome of this design is that part of the roof-top level cabins will be fully covered in grass. This will more than double the size of the open grassed area on the top of Mt Roberts. As in the past, forest-fringed views will be east out over Nixon’s Creek valley towards Ships stern and beyond, as well six new rooms that will have northern views.
132	
133	##### 9. Will the accommodation rooms have ensuites or separate bathroom facilities? What about spa baths?
134	
135	Each room will have its own ensuite toilet and shower facilities. There will not be spa baths in the new rooms to encourage water saving behaviour and differentiation from the value proposition of the Sky Lodges.
136	
137	##### 10. Will there be TVs in the rooms?
138	
139	Yes, all new accommodation rooms will have TV’s. The TV will also provide the opportunity for welcome messages and well as information about Binna Burra and Woonoongoora (Lamington National Park).
140	
141	##### 11. Why is a lift planned for the new building?
142	
143	Under the Disability Discrimination Act 1992, building certifiers and people involved in designing, constructing and managing a building must comply with standards to provide building access to people with disability. Binna Burra has a responsibility under law to ensure that people with disability have dignified, equitable, costeffective and reasonably achievable access to buildings, and facilities and services within buildings. Additionally, the idea of including a lift came from very clear shareholder and stakeholder feedback that the new design must be accessible to wheelchairs and people with a disability. A regular previous complaint from guests was related to Binna Burra‘s lack of access to people with a disability.
144	
145	##### 12. Is there a dining room planned in the new lodge?
146	
147	Yes. There was a strong view from feedback to have a dining room with 270 degree views. Current building regulations will require a lift to such a dining room.
148	
149	##### 13. Will there be a reading room/library in the new lodge?
150	
151	The new Lodge won’t have a separate reading room. Instead, the library on the second floor of Grooms Cottage is likely to stay the same when the new lodge opens in 2026. 152	
153	##### 14. Will guests be able to access rooms and the lodge under shelter?
154	
155	Yes, every accommodation room, and the lodge and the carpark will have sheltered access.
156	
157	##### 15. Will there be a fireplace?
158	
159	Yes. There will be a double sided (indoor/outdoor) fireplace facing the lounge on the ground floor level.
160	
161	##### 16. Will the new lodge have WiFi?
162	
163	Yes. Wi-Fi will be available to guests.
164	
165	##### 17. Will there be a chance to become a ‘Chair-Holder’ again?
166	
167	Yes. Before the bushfire, many people had sponsored a chair in the dining room which included the family name on the rear side. 169	##### 18. Will there be a ‘pool’?
170	
171	No. There has been considerable discussion on this matter. 176	
177	There will be a select few parking spaces close to the lodge rooms for unloading and loading. There will also be an accessible carpark for overnight use. Additionally, there will be open parking spaces along the access road to the lodge.

182	
183	##### 21. What happens to guest activities?
184	
185	One outcome of the master planning process since the fires is a designated Adventure Activities Precinct (AAP) from the saddle down to Bellbird Cliffs and centred around Bellbird Clearing. 188	
189	Whilst BBL will remain connected to the grid for the foreseeable future, there are plans to cover the roofs of the Teahouse and new lodge with solar panels which will be connected to the grid and to batteries. 216	Designing and building a new lodge and accommodation on the Binna Burra Cultural Landscape. Click here to download the background paper.

219	
220	All people who act in a responsible way will be welcome to visit the new lodge and stay in the new accommodation. 221	
222	Our safety and security tasks include:
223	
224	- ensuring guest safety, protection and personal property during their stay
225	- protection of Binna Burra property from hostile actions (theft, acts of vandalism)
226	- maintaining public order and ensuring proper behaviour in all public places at Binna Burra
227	
228	- providing our guests with their required level of peace and privacy during their stay
229	- ensuring the possibility of immediate and effective response in the case of any event that requires the intervention of our staff or representatives of third parties (e.g. police, ambulance, rural fire service, national parks rangers)
230	- guaranteeing proper behaviour, as well as the honesty and integrity of all our staff members.

# binnaburralodge

# Discover spectacular natural beauty

Positioned 800 metres above sea level amidst the sub-tropical rainforest of Woonoongoora – **Lamington National Park** in the **Gold Coast Hinterland**, Binna Burra is centre stage to some of Australia’s most spectacular natural features. 

The unique isolation provides the perfect escape from the stresses of every day life and a chance to get back to basics, interact with nature and experience a freedom and sense of peace that few places can offer.

# accommodation

**Experience total relaxation and reconnect with nature** in the luxurious, fully equipped Tiny Wild Houses. These self-contained dwellings come with all the modern amenities, furnishings and appliances you need to make your stay comfortable and enjoyable.

The Sky Lodges are Binna Burra’s **award-winning accommodation** for those wanting a luxury apartment-style escape. Their one of a kind views are second to none.

The Rainforest Campsite, home to our Safari Tents and Private Bunkrooms, is set high in the rainforest bordering Woonoongoora – **Lamington National Park** with bathroom facilities and BBQ shelters. The Rainforest Campsite features various accommodation types for a **secluded and stress-free camping experience**.

# SPECIALS & packages

Check out our latest special offers and accommodation packages, for some great savings on your next stay!

Having a large body of water nearby could help with the fire approvals and accessing water, if ever needed again for bushfires or other fires. There have always been mixed views on the topic of whether Binna Burra should have a swimming pool for guests. Some shareholder feedback to date has supported including a pool which is appropriate to the overall design and landscape. Nevertheless, considering the cost of construction, the potential for noise by pool users, and the ongoing maintenance costs, the Board has made the decision not to include a swimming pool. Another option was to have some form of infinity rock pool for primarily ‘ornamental’ and fire mitigation purposes rather than for swimming purposes.

However, given there are other fire mitigation measures which can be undertaken (e.g. enhanced sprinkler systems) the Board has resolved not to proceed with a large rock pool but will revive ‘Win’s Garden’ with native plantings and a rock garden that includes a small pond for birds and other small wildlife (‘Win’s Garden’ was a feature of the Binna Burra Cultural Landscape included on the Queensland Heritage Register).

##### 19. How many carparks will there be?

There will be a select few parking spaces close to the lodge rooms for unloading and loading. There will also be an accessible carpark for overnight use. Additionally, there will be open parking spaces along the access road to the lodge.

##### 20. What about Office/Admin staff space

Both the 2008 and current 2022 master plans for Binna Burra have a welcome/reception building in the ‘saddle’ area. The welcome building has been designed to cater for office staff – Senior Management, Finance, Marketing, Reception, Activities etc. The concept is to remove the previous congestion at the Lodge and current congestion at the Teahouse, by having this Welcome Building in the ‘saddle’ – on the left as you enter the Binna Burra Cultural Landscape. As guests arrive they will go to reception in the Welcome Building to check in and then drive to their accommodation (Lodge, Sky Lodges, Tiny Houses, Campground Hill etc), park their car and hopefully then walk around for the duration of their stay. Binna Burra was awarded a $2 million Commonwealth Government grant to build the welcome building and ‘back of house’ (housekeeping and maintenance shed) below the Barn. They were completed and operational in 2024.

##### 21. What happens to guest activities?

One outcome of the master planning process since the fires is a designated Adventure Activities Precinct (AAP) from the saddle down to Bellbird Cliffs and centred around Bellbird Clearing. This will include the via ferrata on the cliff, a new netted activity up in the trees (for ages 3-80+) at the site of the old ropes course and a luge from the saddle down to Bellbird Clearing. The development of a new all-access senses trail is planned. Guest activities will have their independent reception desk within the welcome building.

##### 22. Where does the power come from?

Whilst BBL will remain connected to the grid for the foreseeable future, there are plans to cover the roofs of the Teahouse and new lodge with solar panels which will be connected to the grid and to batteries. In due course, as battery technology continues to improve, Binna Burra would ideally like to be fully powered by solar (with grid back-up).

##### 23. Where does the water for the new lodge come from?

As it has for many years now, Binna Burra water supply is fed from the Coomera River to the tanks just inside the Park where the water is treated. It is then gravity fed downhill to all the buildings and taps at Binna Burra. Whilst the Hydraulics Engineer will review the needs of the new lodge and accommodation, we expect the existing gravity fed pressure will be more than sufficient.

##### 24. What is the indicative timeline for building the new lodge and accommodation?

The current schedule (subject to change):

| **June 2022** | Treasurer announces potential funding support of $18M, BBL apply for RTRP Grant | 
| **Jul – Sep 2022** | Lodge Design Committee (LDC) progresses designs | 
| **Oct 2022 – Jan 2023** | Feedback on two-level Lodge design from shareholders/stakeholders | 
| **Nov 2022** | DTIS approve RTRP Grant of $18M, Agreement signed in Feb 2023 | 
| **Feb – May 2023** | LDC refines design and materials to be as cost-effective as possible | 
| **Jun – Jul 2023** | LDC advises BBL Board that the cost of the current design is still $2.5-$3M more than Grant funds BBL Board considers borrowing extra funds and decides to stay within grant funds for construction BBL Board agrees with LDC proposal to reduce Lodge to one level and keep 30 accommodation rooms | 
| **Aug – Sep 2023** | Feedback on one-level Lodge design from shareholders/stakeholders | 
| **Sep – Oct 2023** | Detailed documentation | 
| **Nov – Dec 2023** | Major building tender to be finalized | 
| **1 Sep 2024** | Building works commence | 
| **May 2026** | Target date for completion of construction | 
| **2026** | Opening of the new Lodge and accommodation | 

##### 25. How has Binna Burra handled the Politics, People, Partners and Process?

**Politics. People. Partners. Process.**

Designing and building a new lodge and accommodation on the Binna Burra Cultural Landscape. Click here to download the background paper.

##### 26. What are the plans for security and access?

All people who act in a responsible way will be welcome to visit the new lodge and stay in the new accommodation. We have the responsibility to provide comfortable and secure accommodation also to guarantee the safety of people and their property staying overnight in any form of accommodation on the Binna Burra Cultural Landscape.

Our safety and security tasks include:

- ensuring guest safety, protection and personal property during their stay
- protection of Binna Burra property from hostile actions (theft, acts of vandalism)
- maintaining public order and ensuring proper behaviour in all public places at Binna Burra

- providing our guests with their required level of peace and privacy during their stay
- ensuring the possibility of immediate and effective response in the case of any event that requires the intervention of our staff or representatives of third parties (e.g. police, ambulance, rural fire service, national parks rangers)
- guaranteeing proper behaviour, as well as the honesty and integrity of all our staff members.

##### 27. Questions of furniture types and layout

The furniture and layout of furniture shown in the plans and fly throughs **are for display purposes only** to give the sense of scale at this stage. The final types of furniture and layouts are yet to be determined. 

##### 28. Can shareholders give further input to the new lodge design?

The design team is always open to ideas and suggestions to help ensure that what we end up with is the best possible outcome for Binna Burra lodge Ltd. Just use the feedback submission form below, or send an email directly to the design team at [email protected]

##### 29. Will there be noise during the construction of the new lodge and accommodation at Mt Roberts?

Our Sky Lodge buildings feature core-filled concrete walls, with all rooms facing north to assist in minimising noise levels. Construction work will begin at 7 am, but to further reduce noise disruptions, the majority of the louder tasks will be scheduled between 10 am and 5 pm. This timing aligns with when most of our guests are out exploring the National Park or enjoying a meal at the Tea House Café.

##### 30. Will the new lodge be air conditioned?

Yes, all accommodation rooms and the lodge dining and lounge rooms will be airconditioned.

##### 31. Will the new buildings include sustainability features like solar or rainwater collection?

Absolutely. The lodge and parts of the accommodation buildings will be fitted with solar panels to help generate electricity, and rainwater from the lodge roof will be harvested and stored.

# How to Get Here

### Our Location

#### Binna Burra Lodge

1069 Binna Burra Road

Beechmont, Queensland

The journey to Binna Burra from Brisbane or the Gold Coast is a convenient and straightforward drive on all–bitumen roads. The drive takes approximately 90 minutes from Brisbane and 40 minutes from the Gold Coast. Upon arrival, you will find yourself 800m above sea level at the end of Binna Burra Road, where you will find Binna Burra Lodge.

Please be aware that there is no public transport available in Binna Burra, and we are not serviced by taxis or ride share. It is important to organise private return transfers prior to your visit.

### By Car

**Binna Burra Lodge is at the end of Binna Burra Road – once you’re on it, please ignore your SAT Nav (and even google maps) – just drive all the way to the end! You’ll know when you’re here!**

**If travelling on the Pacific Motorway (M1):** Take the Nerang exit (exit 69 Southound or exit 73 Northbound) and follow the signs Nerang West/Binna Burra. Take the turn-off to Beechmont and head straight up to the top of the mountain.

**If travelling south from Brisbane** on the Mt Lindsay Highway (Beaudesert Rd), turn left at Jimboomba on to Mundoolun Connection Rd at the service station. On reaching the T intersection, turn left towards Tamborine/Beenleigh; after 2km turn right to Canungra. (If travelling from Beaudesert follow the Gold Coast signs to Canungra.) Once at Canungra, follow the signs 19km to Beechmont and 10km from the roundabout to Binna Burra Lodge.

### Private Transfer

Binna Burra can recommend a private transfer service for you, please call reception on (07) 5533 3622 for details. Pick ups can be arranged from Brisbane and the Gold Coast. Bookings are essential and are on a request basis

### Binna Burra Mountain Lodge & Campsite

1040 Binna Burra Rd

 Beechmont

 Queensland 4211

 Australia

655	# Frequently Asked Questions
656	
657	General
658	
659	##### How do I check-in?
660	
661	Prior to arrival you will receive an online check-in registration document to confirm your reservations details. Once at Binna Burra please visit Reception in the Welcome Building for further check in instructions.
662	
663	##### What hours is your Welcome Building open?
664	
665	Our Welcome Building is open from 8am to 5pm daily, with an extended opening time of 6pm on Fridays. There is a after hours box for returning keys outside of these times at the front of the Binna Burra Tea House.
666	
667	Reception is closed 25 December 2025
668	
669	##### What is your cancellation policy?
670	
671	##### Do I have to stay 2 nights?
672	
673	A 2-night minimum stay applies on Friday and Saturday nights (swag campsites and bunkhouses excluded). Some periods, such as school holidays or long weekends, may occasionally require a longer stay, depending on the time of year. The best way to check is by viewing availability on our website, where any minimum stay restrictions will be clearly displayed.
674	
675	##### How much does it cost to stay per night?
676	
677	We’re always striving to offer the most competitive prices – therefore nightly rates can vary throughout the year and throughout the days of the week. Generally by booking further into the future, and on days which are less popular you’ll secure our lowest pricing.
678	
679	##### When is check in and check out?
680	
681	Check-in is from 2PM. Check-out is 10AM. We are unable to guarantee any check-ins or checkouts earlier or later than these times.
682	
683	##### What if I arrive early can I park my car and go for a walk?
684	
685	Yes, prior to 2pm check-in you can certainly park your vehicle in the day use car parks and visit the national park, Binna Burra Teahouse, or participate in Binna Burra activities. This is also the case after you have checked out of out site at 10am on departure day.
686	
687	##### What is the best way to book? Online or over the phone?
688	
689	Our booking website features 100% of our live availability. We’d recommend booking online to take advantage of our best prices and promotions.
690	
691	##### Can I order breakfast and BBQ packs?
692	
693	Yes, you can! See our dining page for more info on breakfast and BBQ packs + information on how to order them.
694	
695	##### Do you have free WIFI?
696	
697	Your stay at Binna Burra is a chance to unwind and disconnect from the world. However, for those who need to stay connected, we offer complimentary WiFi in the Tea House. Additionally, guests staying in our Sky Lodges and Tiny Wild Houses enjoy free in-room WiFi for added convenience.
698	
699	##### Is there phone reception at Binna Burra?
700	
701	You’ll be pleased to know that phone reception is available at Binna Burra, with Telstra and Optus offering the strongest connection. However, please note that our remote location may cause some patchy coverage from time to time.
702	
703	##### Do you offer EV/Tesla charging stations?
704	
705	Binna Burra offers a Tesla Wall Connector charging station for the convenience of our in-house guests. Note that the charger was installed in 2020, is specifically designed for Tesla vehicles and comes with charger leads that reach 2.4 metres. As of now, we do not provide any adaptors or extensions for other vehicle models.
706	
707	To access the charging station, please speak to our reception team as it is located behind a security boom gate. This amenity is exclusively available to guests staying on-site. So, if you’re planning to stay with us and own a Tesla vehicle, you can take advantage of this eco-friendly charging option during your stay at Binna Burra.
708	
709	##### How can I check the weather at Binna Burra?
710	
711	For real-time weather updates at Binna Burra, you can check our state-of-the-art weather station, located at the Tea House. View live conditions in person on the tablet HUD before setting off on a hike, or access it anytime online at our live weather dashboard.
712	
713	This advanced system tracks everything you’d expect—rain, wind, temperature, humidity—plus a lightning strike tracker, pollen levels, air quality, Air Quality Index (AQI), UV index, and astronomy data.
714	
715	By default, temperatures display in Fahrenheit, but you can easily switch to Celsius:
716	
717	- On mobile – Tap the menu icon (top right), select Settings, then choose Celsius.
718	- On desktop – Click the black cogwheel (top right) to change to Celsius instantly.

721	
722	No, Binna Burra is surrounded by Lamington National Park and therefore no domestic animals are permitted at the property.

Check-in is from 2PM. Check-out is 10AM. We are unable to guarantee any check-ins or checkouts earlier or later than these times.

Yes, prior to 2pm check-in you can certainly park your vehicle in the day use car parks and visit the national park, Binna Burra Teahouse, or participate in Binna Burra activities. This is also the case after you have checked out of out site at 10am on departure day.

Our booking website features 100% of our live availability. We’d recommend booking online to take advantage of our best prices and promotions.

Yes, you can! See our dining page for more info on breakfast and BBQ packs + information on how to order them.

Your stay at Binna Burra is a chance to unwind and disconnect from the world. However, for those who need to stay connected, we offer complimentary WiFi in the Tea House. Additionally, guests staying in our Sky Lodges and Tiny Wild Houses enjoy free in-room WiFi for added convenience.

You’ll be pleased to know that phone reception is available at Binna Burra, with Telstra and Optus offering the strongest connection. However, please note that our remote location may cause some patchy coverage from time to time.

Binna Burra offers a Tesla Wall Connector charging station for the convenience of our in-house guests. By default, temperatures display in Fahrenheit, but you can easily switch to Celsius:

- On mobile – Tap the menu icon (top right), select Settings, then choose Celsius.
- On desktop – Click the black cogwheel (top right) to change to Celsius instantly.

No, Binna Burra is surrounded by Lamington National Park and therefore no domestic animals are permitted at the property.

## PAGE [wedding]: https://www.binnaburralodge.com.au/groomscottage/

# Bushwalker's Bar

**Opening Hours – Bushwalker’s Bar**

Friday & Saturday

**Bar:** 2:00pm – 8:00pm**Dining:** From 3:00pm – 7:30pm

(Hours may vary outside school holiday periods.)

## The Heritage Reading Room

### “Reading is dreaming with eyes wide open”

The upstairs ‘Heritage Reading Room’ of Groom’s Cottage is a collective effort supported by book donations from hundreds of people saddened by the loss of Binna Burra and the old lodge library. There is a plethora of historical items on Binna Burra, Lamington National Park, and the pioneering characters behind their establishment.

Read about the history of Arthur Groom teaming up with bushwalking enthusiast Romeo Lahey, a timber-cutter by trade but also a pioneering environmentalist. Their partnership was equipped with a potent mix of idealism and pragmatism to realise their combined dream. They purchased 34 hectares of land from dairy farmer George Rankin by selling shares in the property and set about establishing a basic holiday camp. They also formed the Queensland National Parks Association to promote the preservation of key environmental areas.

**Reading room open daily for guests. See reception staff for more information.**

# The Heritage Heart

Open daily for guests to enjoy, the upstairs reading room at Groom’s Cottage offers stunning views down the Numinbah Valley and over the Hinze Dam and the distant skyline of the Gold Coast beaches and a cosy space to unwind. Browse the small collection of books available to borrow or settle in for a board game or two – perfect for a quiet afternoon escape.

For those wanting something a little more casual and cosy, stop by the Bushwalker’s Bar for an afternoon drink and pizza on a Friday or Saturday evening, best enjoyed outside at sundown on the terrace or inside for those colder evenings.

**BAR OPENING HOURS:**

Please contact Binna Burra Reception for current hours

- Phone 07 5533 3622

## Share your feedback!

We pride ourselves on providing the best experience possible for all of our guests arriving at the gateway to the Scenic Rim. We would love to hear your feedback from your time spent with us

#### Be a part of our new story

The Groom’s Cottage was the home of Arthur Groom who established Binna Burra Lodge (along with Romeo Lahey). As one of the last remaining heritage buildings at Binna Burra, we had to find a way to open this to the public, so we’ve done just that. We welcome you to join those who have been enjoying the Grooms Cottage for 85 years and be a part of the new history of Binna Burra. Experience some of the most breathtaking scenery from the cottage terrace, enjoy the heritage reading room upstairs and a sundowner or two at the Bushwalkers Bar downstairs.

Check opening times with Binna Burra Reception.

1307	Welcome to Binna Burra, a world-class destination where breathtaking natural wonders await you. We take immense pride in being a cherished heritage-listed destination that offers unforgettable experiences, right here in Woonoongoora, Lamington National Park, Queensland, Australia.
1308	
1309	After facing a challenging period when we had to temporarily close our doors for 12 months starting from 8th September 2019 due to devastating bushfires, we are pleased to announce that Binna Burra is back and better than ever.
1310	
1311	We can’t wait for you to explore our incredible facilities and accommodation. Get ready to be enchanted by our brand new luxurious Tiny Wild Houses, designed to make you feel right at home amidst nature’s embrace. 1313	We invite you to discover the wonders that await in our backyard. Come and experience the warmth, beauty, and friendly hospitality that make us truly special. We can’t wait to welcome you with open arms and share the magic of Binna Burra and the Scenic Rim with you.
1314	
1315	We acknowledge and pay respects to the Yugambeh people of the Gold Coast and all their descendants both past and present. We also acknowledge the many Aboriginal people from other regions as well as Torres Strait and South Sea Islander people who now live in the local area and have made an important contribution to the community.
1316	
1317	## Binna Burra Lodge Mission Statement
1318	
1319	To be a meaningful connection to nature and heritage.
1320	
1321	We attain this by:
1322	
1323	- Providing a gateway to Woonoongoora – Lamington National Park.
1324	- Offering a range of eco-friendly accommodation, activities and experiences.
1325	- Nurturing and improving the land and heritage buildings of which we are the custodians.
1326	
1327	Positioned 800 metres above sea level amidst the sub-tropical rainforest of Woonoongoora – Lamington National Park in the Scenic Rim and Gold Coast Hinterland, Binna Burra is centre stage to some of Australia’s most spectacular natural features.
1328	
1329	Binna Burra also holds the enviable status of being the first Australian property to attain the internationally recognised Green Globe Certification for its best-practice environmental performance, and was listed in the top 10 Eco-Lodges and Green Hotels in the World.
1330	
1331	The unique isolation and idyllic location provide the perfect escape from the stresses of everyday life and a chance to get back to basics, interact with nature and experience a freedom and sense of peace that few places can offer.
1332	
1333	## A Rich History
1334	
1335	One of Australia’s longest-established nature-based resorts, Binna Burra Mountain Lodge was founded in 1933 by Arthur Groom and Romeo Lahey and others who previously (1930) had formed Australia’s first dedicated conservation organisation, the National Parks Association of Queensland. These two pioneering conservationists shared a vision to create a place where people could stay and experience the beauty of the Lamington National Park rainforest. Through interpretive walks and educational programs, they believed more people would become committed to preserving this natural wilderness for future generations. In the early 1930s, they purchased the last freehold title on the boundary of Lamington National Park and formed a public company to fund the establishment of what was to become Binna Burra Mountain Lodge.
1336	
1337	The first Binna Burra camp was held over the Christmas holidays in 1933. Romeo, Arthur and 70 hardy adventurers set up a collection of tents on the “saddle” where the Senses Trail now starts. For five shillings a day, they were provided with accommodation, meals and guided walks through the rainforest. Despite cyclonic storms which ripped through the mountains from Boxing Day until New Year, the camp was declared a success and the decision was made to build permanent cabins on the property.
1338	
1339	An old Canungra boarding house (Leighton House) was dismantled and brought up to Binna Burra by packhorse, to serve as the dining and recreation room. For the cabins, tallow-wood slabs and stringy-bark shingles were hewn from the local timber.
1340	
1341	By Easter 1934, the first hut was nearly finished and, by 1939, Binna Burra Mountain Lodge could accommodate 54 guests. The road was extended in 1947 to eliminate that last 400m trek and a network of walking tracks provided easier access to the rainforest wilderness. The very first track built was to Bellbird Lookout
1342	
1343	Binna Burra quickly became a popular destination with keen bushwalkers of all ages. It also attracted a number of scientists studying the flora and fauna of this living laboratory. Guided, interpretive bushwalks were a feature of the Binna Burra experience even from the earliest days.
1344	
1345	After his initial contribution towards construction and track building, Romeo Lahey remained as a director of the company, on and off, until 1960. As resident manager, Arthur Groom lived on site. He and his wife Marjorie and their three sons, Donn, Tony and Richard, lived in the cabin once also used as the LNHA Environmental Study Centre. Nowadays, Groom’s Cottage houses the Binna Burra Bushwalker’s Bar and, upstairs, the Heritage Reading Room.
1346	
1347	During the late 60s and early 70s, the Lodge was improved and extended using mostly volunteer labour. The ‘Friends of Binna Burra’ (FOBBs) have continued to make a significant contribution over the ensuing years. Another innovation was the introduction of ‘Vacation Schools’. These included the Wildlife Preservation Society Spring School in 1968, the Creative Arts and Photographic Schools in 1969, and Greenfingers’ Week in 1970. The Lodge still hosts a regular program of Special Interest Events every year.
1348	
1349	In 2002, the entire site was designated the Binna Burra Cultural Landscape on the Queensland Heritage Register as a place (a) important in demonstrating the evolution or pattern of Queensland’s history, )b) important because of its aesthetic significance, (c) having a strong or special association with a particular community or cultural group for social, cultural or spiritual reasons and (d) having special association with the life or work of a particular person, group or organisation of importance in Queensland’s history.
1350	
1351	On 8 September 2019, at the beginning of six month of ‘Black Summer’ bushfires across Australia, the central heritage lodge and pioneer cabins, as well as other infrastructure was destroyed or damaged. The site was closed for 12 months and reopened for trading with the remaining assets in September 2020.
1352	
1353	“Binna Burra to me is more than home. It is more than a lifetime commitment. It is a feeling, a spirit, a way of life. It is also a sum of all those who have worked there or stayed as a guest. My hope is that an unchanged Binna Burra, the place and the spirit, will outlive me and my children.”
1354	
1355	Marjorie Groom (1911-1998) with Richard Groom, Donn Groom & Tony Groom. *Photo circa 1940s.*
1356	
1357	
1358	## Our Commitment To Sustainability
1359	
1360	### Sustainability Overview
1361	
1362	Binna Burra’s Board and staff are fully committed to implementing and demonstrating effective sustainable management. We have been doing this since the company was first formed in the 1930s, and over the past 20 years, we have pioneered many practices which are now part of international sustainable tourism guidelines.
1363	
1364	We aim to achieve the international standards for sustainable tourism laid out by the Global Sustainable Tourism Council (GSTC) in order to ensure our business operations:
1365	
1366	- Maximise social and economic benefits to the local community and minimize any negative impacts
1367	- Maximise benefits to our cultural heritage and minimise any negative impacts
1368	- Maximise benefits to our world heritage listed natural environment and minimise negative impacts
1369	
1370	As an example, by designing and adopting site-specific best practice procedures as detailed in the Lodge’s Environmental Management Plan (EMP), Binna Burra has dramatically reduced its environmental impacts and has also benefited financially from the reductions in energy usage.
1371	
1372	This effort was so significant that Binna Burra Mountain Lodge first earned Green Globe Certification in 2001. In doing so, Binna Burra was also the first private company in Australasia to achieve certification under the international Green Globe standards for sustainable tourism practices.
1373	
1374	Prior to and since its certification, Binna Burra had been recognised by a variety of environmental, ecotourism and tourism organisations. In 2018 during the annual conference of Ecotourism Australia held in Townsville, Binna Burra was one of a handful of Australian tourism enterprises recognised for 20 consecutive years of maintaining its ecotourism certification.
1375	
1376	Binna Burra Lodge Ltd has committed to benchmarking its energy and water consumption, total waste production and community commitment; along with implementing an integrated environmental and social policy.
1377	
1378	The GSTC establishes and manages global sustainable standards, known as the GSTC Criteria. These are the guiding principles and minimum international requirements that any tourism business or destination should aspire to reach in order to protect and sustain the world’s natural and cultural resources while ensuring tourism meets its potential as a tool for conservation and poverty alleviation.
1379	
1380	“Binna Burra Lodge has had what we now call a **sustainable** approach to tourism since its inception in 1933 when the concept of **national parks** was still new around the world.
1381	
1382	Nowadays we also have the framework of **world heritage values**. This results in Binna Burra Lodge sharing responsibility for conservation of our **cultural and natural heritage** through **sustainable tourism management**.”
1383	
1384	## **Acknowledging the earliest inhabitants at Binna Burra**
1385	
1386	*A statement of information and policy endorsed by the Board of Directors,* *Binna Burra Lodge Limited, 18 December 2017.*
1387	
1388	*‘Lamington National Park’s earliest human inhabitants were an Aboriginal kinship group, the Yugambeh who lived in this area, carefully managing and using its rich natural resources. Known as ‘Woonoongoora’ to the Yugambeh, the mountains are sacred and spiritual, places to be nurtured and respected.’*
1389	
1390	*Dept of Environment and Science (DES)*
1391	
1392	As a business that operates within a World Heritage designated natural environment, Binna Burra Lodge Limited’s vision ‘To be a meaningful connection to nature and heritage’ is delivered with the identification, protection, conservation, presentation and transmission to future generations of the cultural and natural heritage of our location.
1393	
1394	We acknowledge and respect that the land upon which Binna Burra is located was used by traditional ‘first nations’ people of this mountain area.
1395	
1396	*While some people may see Acknowledgement and Welcome to Country as a recent practice invented for the sake of political correctness, or an empty token gesture, Wurundjeri Elder, Joy Murphy Wandin, describes it as “a very important way of giving Aboriginal people back their place in society, and an opportunity for us to say, ‘We are real, we are here, and today we welcome you to our land’…It’s paying respect, in a formal sense, and following traditional custom in a symbolic way.”*
1397	
1398	https://australianstogether.org.au/resources-2/welcome-to-and-acknowledgement-of-country/

1400	## Lamington Natural History Association (LNHA)
1401	
1402	
1403	**In 1975 the Lamington Natural History Association (LNHA) was formed, in association with Binna Burra Mountain Lodge, O’Reilly’s Rainforest Guesthouse and the Queensland National Parks and Wildlife Service.**
1404	
1405	LNHA was based on a concept which was common in the USA in the early 1970s, but was the first of its type in Australia. One of the Association’s early major projects was the establishment of an environmental study centre and headquarters on the Binna Burra property by renovating the timber cabin which Arthur Groom had built for himself and his wife in 1935. Opened in 1976, the centre contained an office, class-room, and dormitory accommodation for children taking part in educational camps (Stubbs & Specht, 2005).
1406	
1407	 The aim of LNHA is, to encourage an understanding and appreciation of the environment and national park values and provide interpretative information for visitors to Lamington National Park.
1408	
1409	 It does this by:
1410	
1411	 • Accredited members assisting the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service (QPWS) by volunteering in the Binna Burra Information Centre on weekends and school holidays
1412	
1413	 • The LNHA provides interpretive information to visitors to Lamington National Park through, Books Track Guides and Brochures
1414	
1415	 • Activities for Members and guests on four weekends per year
1416	
1417	 • Guest speakers provide specialist talks on topics relating to Natural History, the environment and Lamington National Park
1418	
1419	## **National Parks Association of Queensland (NPAQ)**
1420	
1421	**Back in 1930, the pioneering founders of Binna Burra, Romeo Lahey and Arthur Groom were also instrumental in the founding of the NPAQ.**
1422	
1423	 It was out of the NPAQ and its increasingly popular camp-outs that the idea of establishing low-cost but comfortable accommodation which would allow a greater number of people to gain access to the peace, freedom and beauty of Queensland’s national parks emerged, and Binna Burra was established in 1933. The association continues to promote the preservation, expansion and good management of national parks and other forms of protected areas in Queensland.
1424	
1425	 ‘During the early years of Binna Burra, (Romeo) Lahey also marked out and began construction of walking tracks within Lamington National Park, laying the foundation of the extensive network of tracks in the park today.’ (Stubbs & Specht, 2005)
1426	
1427	 NPAQ is an independent, not-for-profit, membership-based organization, and is the first conservation organisation in Queensland, and the longest running National Park Association in Australia.
1428	
1429	 Nowadays, Binna Burra still shares the objectives of NPAQ:
1430	
1431	 **1)** To preserve the National Parks and other protected areas of Queensland in their natural condition, to the greatest possible extent, and to endeavour to ensure the reservation and preservation of other areas considered to be suitable for protection;
1432	
1433	 **2)** To foster member and public interest in, enjoyment of, and respect for National Parks and nature conservation;
1434	
1435	 **3)** To promote the appropriate management of National Parks and other protected areas, and appropriate management of environmental factors which may affect existing and potential National Parks;
1436	
1437	 **4)** To promote effective legal and environmental protections in respect of National Parks and other protected areas, and to ensure the enforcement of provisions for their protection;
1438	
1439	 **5)** To promote appropriate and balanced measures for visitors to experience National Parks while conserving and protecting the natural environment.
